Source: https://github.com/markziemann/bioinformatics_intro_workshop

## Introduction

Here we will be focusing on prokaryote genome assembly and pangenome analysis.
This will show us the similarities and differences between bacterial isolates,
focusing on gene presence/absence which is generally more important than
characterisation of SNVs between isolates.

The general steps for short reads are:

1. Sequence QC

2. Assembly with Unicycler

3. Genome annotation with Prokka

4. Pangenome analysis with Roary

5. Downstream analysis

For sequence of individual viral genomes, you might want to try a different pipeline:

1. Sequence QC with FastQC

2. Map reads to reference genome with bwa/minibwa generating SAM files

3. Convert the SAM to BAM with SamTools

4. Generate mpileup file and call variants using BCFtools

## Prerequisites

I'm working on a server with Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS or higher LTS installed.

Packages needed are `fastqc`, `multiqc`, `unicycler`, `roary`.

If you want to run jobs in parallel, then it is recommended to install GNU parallel as well.

We will also need conda to install `prokka`.

```{bash,install,eval = FALSE}
sudo apt install fastqc multiqc unicycler prokka
sudo apt install parallel
```

## Tmux: a recommendation

Wherever possible, you should be using `tmux` to manage your sessions as
this workflow has some long running steps.

A reminder on how to use it

```{bash,tmuxuse,eval=FALSE}
# new session
tmux new -s patho
# disconnect session
tmux detach
# re-attach
tmux attach -t patho
# emergency kill
tmux kill-session -t patho
```

## Download a copy of the data

Location: https://ziemann-lab.net/public/bioinfo_workshop/2026/pathogen_seq/rawdata/

These are real Salmonella enterica datasets from clinical samples and from environmental samples
like poultry farms.

Some of this data has been published [here](https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S2165049722007454).

```{bash,seqdl,eval=FALSE}
if [ ! -d rawdata ] ; then
  DIRURL=https://ziemann-lab.net/public/bioinfo_workshop/2026/pathogen_seq/rawdata
  mkdir rawdata
  cd rawdata
  wget -N $DIRURL/100346_R1.fq.gz
  wget -N $DIRURL/100346_R2.fq.gz
  wget -N $DIRURL/100347_R1.fq.gz
  wget -N $DIRURL/100347_R2.fq.gz
  wget -N $DIRURL/100348_R1.fq.gz
  wget -N $DIRURL/100348_R2.fq.gz
  wget -N $DIRURL/100349_R1.fq.gz
  wget -N $DIRURL/100349_R2.fq.gz
  cd -
fi

du -sh rawdata/*
```

## Run Quality control analysis

I like to use [FastQC](https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/)
for basic sequence quality control and then [MultiQC](https://github.com/MultiQC/MultiQC)
for assembling all the reports into one convenient page.

Here is the script that I use called `run_fastqc.sh`.
As you can see there is a version that runs one fastqc job at a time, and another
that uses GNU parallel to run 4 jobs at once, each with up to 4 threads.

Use `top` to monitor how CPU resources are being used.

Do not exceed the number of CPU threads on your system.

```{bash,qc1,eval=FALSE}
#!/bin/bash

# run fastqc on the fastq files
# FastQC v0.11.5
for FQZ in *.fq.gz ; do
  echo $FQZ
  fastqc -t 4 $FQZ
done

# get it done 4x faster
#ls *fq.gz | parallel -j4 fastqc -t4 {}

# multiqc, version 1.7
multiqc .
```

When this script runs, you will see stderr from fastQC and then from multiQC,
telling you whether it has completed successfully.

You will also see insdividual QC reports for each fastq file.
These are not very helpful, as there are so many.
It is preferred to use multiQC to aggregate the findings into a single report.

If you are running this analysis on your own laptop, you will be able to open up
the html and view the results.
If you are using a workstation or HPC via ssh, then you will need to copy the data
to your local system first.

You can see the report that I prepared previously [here](https://ziemann-lab.net/public/bioinfo_workshop/2026/pathogen_seq/multiqc_report.html).

What we want to look for is:

* Total sequence output/coverage - should be 30 genome coverage at least

* Unique vs duplicated reads - duplicated reads are not informative

* Sequence quality along the read length - any sudden drops or anomalies

* GC content smooth - deviations from bell curve could suggest problems in library prep

* Sequence duplication - presence of contaminating sequences

* Adapter content - adapters could reduce the assembly performance

## Assembly

Here we are using [Unicycler](https://github.com/rrwick/Unicycler) to guide the assembly of short reads.

I like to create a new folder called `assembly` and link the fastq files there with `ln -s origin destination`.

Here is the script that I call `run_unicycler.sh`:

```{bash,unicycler,eval=FALSE}
#!/bin/bash

#unicycler -1 short_reads_1.fastq.gz -2 short_reads_2.fastq.gz -o output_dir
#unicycler  -1 100346_R1.fq.gz  -2 100346_R2.fq.gz  -o 100346

for FQZ1 in *_R1.fq.gz ; do
  FQZ2=$(echo $FQZ1 | sed 's/_R1.fq.gz/_R2.fq.gz/' )
  PFX=$(echo $FQZ1 | cut -d '_' -f1)
  echo $FQZ1 $FQZ2 $PFX
  unicycler  -1 $FQZ1 -2 $FQZ2  -o $PFX
done
```

Unicycler is a bit slow, so we won't be able to run all 4 assemblies in the workshop session.

But the assembly data have been uploaded for you to use [here](https://ziemann-lab.net/public/bioinfo_workshop/2026/pathogen_seq/assembly/).

We should inspect contigs generated.

```
zgrep '>' 100346/assembly.fasta.gz
```

You will see that there is a circular contig:

```
>48 length=11069 depth=3.63x circular=true
```

You may also see sequences that are amplified:

```
>70 length=1295 depth=14.37x
```

Which could be a repetitive element or a prophage.

Contigs can be extracted

```
samtools faidx assembly.fasta 48
samtools faidx assembly.fasta 70
```

Further quality control of assemblies is recommended using [QUAST](https://github.com/ablab/quast)
which will calculate N50 and a range of other quality metrics.

## Genome annotation with Prokka

Prokka is a program for rapid prokaryotic genome annotation.

```{bash,prokka_setup_conda,eval=FALSE}
conda deactivate
conda create -n prokka bioconda::prokka
conda activate prokka
prokka --version
```

There is a bug in this version which can be fixed using nano:

```{bash,dumb_bug_fix,eval=FALSE}
nano /home/mark.ziemann@domain.internal.burnet.edu.au/miniconda3/envs/prokka/bin/prokka
```

Change this section:

```
  'blastp' => {
    GETVER  => "blastp -version",
    REGEXP  => qr/blastp:\s+($BIDEC)/,
    MINVER  => "2.2",
    NEEDED  => 1,
  },
```

So it looks like this:

```
  'blastp' => {
    GETVER  => "blastp -version",
    REGEXP  => qr/blastp:\s+($BIDEC)/,
    MINVER  => "2.12",
    NEEDED  => 1,
  },
```

And the same for makeblastdb.

Then we can use the script `run_prokka.sh`.

```{bash,run_prokka,eval=FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
for FA in *fa ; do
  PFX=$(echo $FA | sed 's/.fa//')
  echo $PFX
  prokka --force --outdir $PFX --genus Salmonella --species enterica --kingdom Bacteria  $FA
done
```

You will get the following files appearig in your output folder:


## Run pangenome analysis with Roary

I have prepared some Prokka annotation files available [here](https://ziemann-lab.net/public/bioinfo_workshop/2026/pathogen_seq/annotations/).

You can download those and run the following command to kick-off the pangenome analysis.

```
roary -p 8 -e -n -v -f roary_output *gff
```

The output directory should have the following

```
.
├── accessory_binary_genes.fa
├── accessory_binary_genes.fa.newick
├── accessory_graph.dot
├── accessory.header.embl
├── accessory.tab
├── blast_identity_frequency.Rtab
├── clustered_proteins
├── core_accessory_graph.dot
├── core_accessory.header.embl
├── core_accessory.tab
├── core_alignment_header.embl
├── core_gene_alignment.aln
├── gene_presence_absence.csv
├── gene_presence_absence.Rtab
├── number_of_conserved_genes.Rtab
├── number_of_genes_in_pan_genome.Rtab
├── number_of_new_genes.Rtab
├── number_of_unique_genes.Rtab
├── pan_genome_reference.fa
└── summary_statistics.txt

1 directory, 20 files
```

The summary_statistics.txt shows the number of core and accessory genes.

The newick tree can be pasted into online tree viewers like [this one](https://etetoolkit.org/treeview/)
This shows the relative similarity of gene sets across isolates.

The `gene_presence_absence.Rtab` file is another interesting one that shows the gene presence and
absence across isolated.

Here is how we can visualise the gene presence and absence using a heatmap in R.

```{r,read_rtab,eval=FALSE}
library("gplots")

x <- read.table("gene_presence_absence.Rtab",header=TRUE)
dim(x)

mx <- as.matrix(head(x,1000))

colfunc <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))

colnames(mx) <- sapply(strsplit(colnames(mx),"_"),"[[",1)

heatmap.2( mx , col=colfunc(25),scale="none",
    trace="none",margins = c(6,6),
    cexRow=0.4, cexCol=0.5,
    main="Gene presence/absence")
```

## Running a core gene alignment

This is not normally required, but here is how to do it.
First extract the core genes of interest.

This is a script called `extract_prot.sh` which outputs protein sequences
to the stdout.

```
#!/bin/bash
#aroC|dnaN|hemD|hisD|purE|sucA|thrA

for GFF in */*.gff ; do

  ISOLATE=$(echo $GFF | cut -d '/' -f1)
  FAA=$(echo $GFF | sed 's/.gff/.faa/')

  perl unwrap_fasta.pl $FAA - > tmp && mv tmp $FAA

  echo $ISOLATE >&2

  for GENE in aroC dnaN hemD hisD purE sucA thrA  ; do

    GENECNT=$(grep -wc $GENE $GFF)

    echo $GENE >&2

    if [ $GENECNT -gt 0 ] ; then

      LOCTAG=$(grep -w $GENE $GFF | sed 's/locus_tag=/@/' \
      | cut -d '@' -f2 | cut -d ';' -f1)

      SEQNAME=${GENE}_${ISOLATE}
      grep -A1 $LOCTAG $FAA | paste - - | cut -f2 \
      | sed "s/^/>${SEQNAME}\t/" | tr '\t' '\n'

    fi
  done
done
```

It is used like this:

```
 ./extract_prot.sh > protein.fa
```

Then we can use another script to conduct the clustal alignment:

```
for GENE in aroC dnaN hemD hisD purE sucA thrA ; do

  grep -A1 $GENE protein.fa | grep -v '\--' > $GENE.fa

  clustalo -i $GENE.fa -o $GENE.aln --guidetree-out=${GENE}.tree  --outfmt=clustal -v --force

done
```

In our case, there were only a few SNPs observed in these core genes, so it wasn't informative.
